title: Deterministic Verification and a Single‑Repair Guardrail for LLM‑Generated Network Configurations: a Paired, Shared‑Candidate Study
abstract: We report a preregistered, artifact-backed paired experiment that measured the verifier-confirmed effect of inserting a deterministic validator plus up to one automated repair (a guarded generate–verify–repair pipeline) on the same LLM-generated configuration candidate. Under preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics we generated a single initial candidate per natural-language intent with gpt-5-mini for N = 250 intent pairs (confirmatory partition: synthetic/emulation only) and evaluated two episodes per intent: baseline (accept candidate as-is) and guarded (run deterministic validator deterministic_netops_validator_v5; if it failed, permit one automated repair attempt). Execution produced 500 completed episodes; model_calls_used = 251 (250 shared initial generations + 1 repair). Results: baseline verifier-pass 249/250 (99.6%), guarded verifier-pass 250/250 (100.0%); paired contingency n11 = 249, n10 = 1, n01 = 0, n00 = 0; paired difference (guarded − baseline) = +0.4 percentage points, 95% CI [0.0, 1.2 pp] (paired bootstrap percentile, 10,000 resamples, seed = 1729), exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. The single discordant pair was converted to pass by the single permitted repair. We explicitly reconcile provider-call accounting and shared_initial_candidate semantics in Methods, state confirmatory scope (synthetic/emulation partition only), and discuss construct and external limitations. Preregistration and execution artifacts are archived and referenced in the Disclosure Statement.

sections.introduction: Generative large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed to translate operator intent into device configurations for NetOps, but stochastic generation raises operational correctness and safety concerns. Prior work proposes inserting deterministic validators and repair loops between stochastic generators and acceptance (generate–verify–repair, GVR) to detect and correct mechanically verifiable defects; evaluations and surveys report benefits for syntactic and locally checkable errors while noting open challenges for semantic correctness and production heterogeneity [1]–[6]. We preregistered and executed a confirmatory paired experiment under shared_initial_candidate semantics that isolates the marginal verifier+single-repair effect on identical generated candidates. Our contributions are: (1) a preregistered, artifact-backed paired evaluation using gpt-5-mini and a deterministic validator on N = 250 intent pairs (confirmatory partition = synthetic/emulation only); (2) a strict shared_initial_candidate execution and exact paired inference that isolates validator+repair effects on the same initial LLM output; and (3) an evidence-grounded near‑null primary result together with explicit reconciliation of preregistration, execution accounting, and statistical interpretation.
sections.related_work: Studies of intent→configuration systems and NetOps automation show that LLMs can produce draft configurations but typically require verification or human oversight; reported error modes include syntax, local-policy violations, and vendor-CLI subtleties [1], [5]. Architectures that interpose deterministic checkers and repair loops reduce mechanically verifiable defects in code and configuration domains in prior work [2], [3], [5]; however, semantic/behavioral correctness, cross-vendor fidelity, and adversarial robustness remain open. Mature deterministic network analyzers and formal-analysis methods (e.g., Batfish-style analyses, header-space approaches, model-checking) are commonly used as validators in both research and operational tooling [4]. Threat analyses demonstrate prompt-injection and retrieval-attacks against LLM-integrated pipelines and motivate verifier and filter layers as partial mitigations [6]. This study builds on these threads by executing a sealed, preregistered, shared-candidate comparison that measures the verifier-detected marginal benefit of a single permitted automated repair.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and estimand: The study was preregistered as study-cand-2026-LLM-verifier-sim2real-v1. The preregistration specified generation_semantics = shared_initial_candidate (one initial candidate per intent shared across paired episodes), a confirmatory paired design with N_pairs = 250, and the primary estimand paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline. The preregistration enumerated three partitions (emulation/synthetic, community, production-like) but the confirmatory contract and task_count = 250 were applied to the synthetic/emulation partition only; community and production-like partitions were exploratory and were not executed in the confirmatory run. Task generation and candidate generation: a deterministic task generator produced 250 constrained intent tasks. For each intent we generated a single shared initial response using declared model gpt-5-mini; that same candidate was used to evaluate two episodes: baseline (accepted as-is; no repair) and guarded (deterministic validator deterministic_netops_validator_v5 run; if validator failed, permit a single automated repair attempt). Execution contract and calls: preregistered maximum_model_calls = 500 with up to one repair call per episode. Scoring and inference: the validator returned a boolean verifier_pass per episode; primary test was exact McNemar two-sided on paired contingency counts; 95% CI used paired bootstrap percentile (10,000 resamples, bootstrap_seed = 1729). Missingness and exclusions: preregistered exclusion rules (parser-blocking syntax, credential tokens, private-address blocks) were applied; no exclusions occurred. Reconciliation of provider-call accounting and shared_initial_candidate semantics: archived execution manifests show completed_episode_count = 500 and complete_pair_count = 250 while model_calls_used = 251. These numbers reconcile as follows (all values are taken from archived execution manifests and deterministic reconciliation): 250 shared_initial_generation model calls produced one candidate per intent that was reused for both baseline and guarded episodes; a single repair call occurred on one guarded episode, producing model_calls_used = 250 + 1 = 251. The manifest's provider_call_audit.stage_counts recorded {"shared_initial_generation": 250, "repair": 1}; provider_call_audit.condition_counts labeled counts per instrumented stage ("shared":250 corresponds to the shared_initial_generation stage calls; "guarded":1 corresponds to the single repair-stage call) and should not be interpreted as independent first‑pass generation counts per condition. The execution manifest and deterministic reconciliation (execution/execution_manifest.json and analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json in the archived bundle) contain the full provider-call audit and stage counts for verification.
sections.results: Execution and accounting: planned_episode_count = 500 (250 pairs × 2 episodes); completed_episode_count = 500; complete_pair_count = 250; model_calls_used = 251 (250 shared initial generations + 1 repair). Primary confirmatory outcome (archived analysis artifacts): baseline_success_count = 249 (0.996), guarded_success_count = 250 (1.0). Paired contingency (guarded, baseline): n11 = 249, n10 = 1, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.004 (0.4 percentage points). Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.0, 0.012] (0 – 1.2 percentage points) based on 10,000 resamples with seed = 1729. Repair outcomes: the single discordant pair (the only n10 cell) was converted to pass by the single permitted automated repair (repair-conversion = 1/250). No preregistered exclusions, contamination flags, or missing pairs occurred. All numeric values, contingency counts, and condition summaries are taken directly from archived analysis artifacts (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv; analysis/condition_summary.csv) and the deterministic reconciliation manifest.
sections.discussion: Interpretation: the preregistered primary hypothesis (anticipating a substantial sim-to-real paired deficit) is not supported for the executed confirmatory partition: in these constrained synthetic/emulation tasks gpt-5-mini produced initial candidates that were already largely consistent with the deterministic validator encodings. Alternative readings are plausible: (A) the task generator and validator encoded mechanically checkable properties for which modern LLMs perform well; (B) the confirmatory partition and the single-repair policy limited observable failure mass; or (C) model selection and prompt design produced unusually high baseline pass rates relative to preregistered power assumptions. Power and inferential constraints: the preregistered power calculation assumed baseline pass ≈ 0.90 and targeted a 15-percentage-point effect; the observed baseline pass rate (0.996) is far higher, so the run has low sensitivity to detect small paired differences and the observed 95% CI upper bound of 1.2 percentage points is the appropriate bound on the paired improvement under the study's design. Threats to validity: internal — results depend on chosen prompt templates, declared model, single-repair policy, and strict shared_initial_candidate semantics; construct — the deterministic validator checked mechanically verifiable workflow and syntactic properties but not broader semantic behavior (protocol dynamics, emergent interactions); external — confirmatory evaluation was limited to the synthetic/emulation partition; community and production-like partitions were not executed in this run and remain exploratory. Security and adversarial limits: adaptive prompt-injection, retrieval-based attacks, vendor-specific CLI subtleties, and heterogeneous real production topologies were not exercised and remain open directions. Operational implication: in similarly constrained emulation-style tasks a guarded GVR pipeline may yield small marginal verifier gains because modern LLMs already produce largely validator-consistent candidates; do not generalize this conclusion beyond the studied regime without partition-specific evidence.
sections.conclusion: We executed a sealed, preregistered paired experiment under shared_initial_candidate semantics to measure the verifier-detected marginal benefit of deterministic validation plus a single automated repair on identical LLM-generated configuration candidates. In N = 250 constrained synthetic intent tasks, initial gpt-5-mini candidates passed the deterministic validator in 249/250 cases and the guarded pipeline converted the single failing candidate; paired improvement = 0.4 percentage points (95% CI [0.0, 1.2 pp], p = 1.0). The preregistered near‑null result implies that GVR-style guardrails can provide limited marginal verifier benefit in some tightly constrained NetOps task regimes; broader, adversarial, and production-like settings require additional, partition-specific study. All execution manifests, raw outputs, validator traces, repair traces, and analysis artifacts are archived as described in the Disclosure Statement.

disclosure_statement: This study was executed autonomously after an autonomy lock under the CNSM Agentic AI Researcher track. Human role: the Research Director selected the broad topic family (Generative AI and LLMs for NetOps) and performed pre-lock infrastructure development only; no human edited technical manuscript content after the autonomy lock. Models and tools (essential): declared model = gpt-5-mini (provider recorded as openai_responses); deterministic validator = deterministic_netops_validator_v5; deterministic task generator = deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5; adapter_family = hosted_netops_gvr_v1. Preregistration: study id = study-cand-2026-LLM-verifier-sim2real-v1; preregistration artifact SHA-256 = 7a984dbf7265c9a774eaf95c6c930dcf5f1e8845088bbc0e0855e3b4f1000ede. Immutable master prompt used to initiate the autonomous run: provenance/master_prompt.txt, SHA-256 = 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba. Autonomy boundary: literature search, design, preregistration freeze, prompt preservation, model calls, deterministic validation, permitted repair execution, analysis, drafting, peer-review, revision, and finalization were performed autonomously after the lock. Execution and analysis artifacts (manifests, raw outputs, validator traces, repair traces, and analysis results) are archived in the evidence bundle referenced by the preregistration manifest; the Disclosure Statement identifies the required immutable prompt and preregistration hashes but does not duplicate full provenance logs here.
limitations: Confirmatory scope: the executed confirmatory run covered the synthetic/emulation partition only per the preregistration; community and production-like partitions listed in the preregistration were not executed in this confirmatory run and remain exploratory.

Validator coverage: the deterministic validator assessed mechanically verifiable properties (syntax and prescribed workflow sequences); broader semantic correctness (protocol dynamics, performance, emergent interactions) was not assessed.
Model and tooling scope: a single declared model (gpt-5-mini) and one validator implementation were used; results do not establish multi-model or alternate-validator generality.

Adversary and retrieval attacks: adaptive prompt-injection, retrieval-based attacks, vendor-targeted exploit vectors, and heterogeneous real-world topologies were not evaluated and remain open threats.
Repair policy: only one automated repair attempt was permitted by design; multi-iteration repair loops, human-in-the-loop escalation, or different repair templates may change outcomes.
